# `silk/text/edit_distance`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Edit distances: the smallest number of single-character edits that turn one text into another.

## When to use
Use these functions to find the closest spelling to a misspelled name, such as a suggestion
for an unknown command-line option, to rank fuzzy search results, or to find near-duplicate
keys. [`damerauLevenshtein`](#damerauLevenshtein) is the usual choice for typing errors, because a swap of two
neighbouring characters, such as `nmae` for `name`, counts as one edit.

## Details
Each function counts four kinds of edit: insert one character, delete one character, replace
one character, and swap two neighbouring characters.

- [`damerauLevenshtein`](#damerauLevenshtein) is the true Damerau-Levenshtein distance. An edit can change text
  that an earlier edit made, so `ca` to `abc` is two edits: swap to `ac`, then insert `b`.
- [`optimalStringAlignment`](#optimalStringAlignment) does not edit a substring more than once, so `ca` to `abc` is
  three edits. It is a little faster, and it is the variant that many libraries call
  "Damerau-Levenshtein".

The `string` forms count Unicode scalar values. The `Bytes` forms count bytes, which is
faster and correct for ASCII text, identifiers, and binary data.

The distances are symmetric, and they are zero only for equal inputs. The text that the two
inputs share at the start and at the end is skipped before the main work. Both functions
use memory proportional to the shorter length. [`damerauLevenshtein`](#damerauLevenshtein) takes time proportional
to the product of the two lengths. [`optimalStringAlignment`](#optimalStringAlignment) processes 64 characters of the
shorter input at a time with bit operations, so it is much faster on long inputs. Inputs of
at most 64 characters each, after the shared start and end, do not allocate.

## Examples
### Suggest the closest known name
```silk
import silk.text.edit_distance
import silk.mem.allocator { Allocator, OutOfMemoryError }
import silk.core.effect { Effect }

effect fn suggest() -> i32 ! OutOfMemoryError ? &mut Allocator {
  let known = ["build", "check", "format", "test"]
  let written = "fromat"
  let mut best: usize = 0
  let mut bestDistance = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshtein(written, known[0])
  let mut at: usize = 1
  while at < known.length {
    let distance = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshtein(written, known[at])
    if distance < bestDistance {
      best = at
      bestDistance = distance
    }
    at = at + 1
  }
  if best != 2 || bestDistance != 1 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}

effect fn exhausted(error: OutOfMemoryError) -> i32 {
  drop error
  return 2
}

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let mut allocator = Allocator.systemAllocatorProvider()
  return run Effect.catchAll(suggest(), exhausted) |> Effect.provideMut<Allocator>(&mut allocator)
}
```

## `damerauLevenshtein`

```silk
pub effect fn damerauLevenshtein(left: string, right: string) -> usize
  ! OutOfMemoryError
  ? &mut Allocator
```

Returns the Damerau-Levenshtein distance between `left` and `right`, counted in Unicode scalar
values.

### When to use

Use this function to measure how far apart two texts are when people type them, for example to
suggest the closest known name for a misspelled one.

### Details

The result is the smallest number of edits that turn `left` into `right`. An edit inserts,
deletes, or replaces one scalar value, or swaps two neighbouring scalar values. Later edits can
change text that earlier edits made, so `"ca"` to `"abc"` is 2. The time is proportional to the
product of the lengths and the memory to the shorter length.

### Errors

- `OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot supply the scratch rows. ASCII inputs of at
  most 64 bytes each, after the shared start and end, do not allocate.

### Gotchas

A scalar value is not always one visible character: `"é"` written as `e` followed by a
combining accent is two scalar values. Normalize both texts first if that matters.

### Examples

#### Count a swap as one edit

```silk
import silk.text.edit_distance
import silk.mem.allocator { Allocator, OutOfMemoryError }
import silk.core.effect { Effect }

effect fn check() -> i32 ! OutOfMemoryError ? &mut Allocator {
  let swapped = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshtein("nmae", "name")
  let replaced = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshtein("café", "cafe")
  let rebuilt = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshtein("ca", "abc")
  if swapped != 1 || replaced != 1 || rebuilt != 2 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}

effect fn exhausted(error: OutOfMemoryError) -> i32 {
  drop error
  return 2
}

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let mut allocator = Allocator.systemAllocatorProvider()
  return run Effect.catchAll(check(), exhausted) |> Effect.provideMut<Allocator>(&mut allocator)
}
```

## `damerauLevenshteinBytes`

```silk
pub effect fn damerauLevenshteinBytes(left: &[u8], right: &[u8]) -> usize
  ! OutOfMemoryError
  ? &mut Allocator
```

Returns the Damerau-Levenshtein distance between `left` and `right`, counted in bytes.

### When to use

Use this function for ASCII text, identifiers, and binary data. For text that can contain other
characters, use [`damerauLevenshtein`](#damerauLevenshtein), which counts Unicode scalar values.

### Details

The result is the smallest number of edits that turn `left` into `right`. An edit inserts,
deletes, or replaces one byte, or swaps two neighbouring bytes. Later edits can change bytes
that earlier edits made, so `ca` to `abc` is 2. The time is proportional to the product of the
lengths and the memory to the shorter length.

### Errors

- `OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot supply the scratch rows. Inputs of at most 64
  bytes each, after the shared start and end, do not allocate.

### Examples

#### Measure two byte strings

```silk
import silk.text.edit_distance
import silk.mem.allocator { Allocator, OutOfMemoryError }
import silk.core.effect { Effect }

effect fn check() -> i32 ! OutOfMemoryError ? &mut Allocator {
  let swapped = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshteinBytes(b"--relaese", b"--release")
  let plural = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshteinBytes(b"dependency", b"dependencies")
  let empty = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshteinBytes(b"", b"abc")
  if swapped != 1 || plural != 3 || empty != 3 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}

effect fn exhausted(error: OutOfMemoryError) -> i32 {
  drop error
  return 2
}

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let mut allocator = Allocator.systemAllocatorProvider()
  return run Effect.catchAll(check(), exhausted) |> Effect.provideMut<Allocator>(&mut allocator)
}
```

<a id="optimalStringAlignment"></a>

## `optimalStringAlignment`

```silk
pub effect fn optimalStringAlignment(left: string, right: string) -> usize
  ! OutOfMemoryError
  ? &mut Allocator
```

Returns the optimal string alignment distance between `left` and `right`, counted in Unicode
scalar values.

### When to use

Use this function when the variant of Damerau-Levenshtein distance that many other libraries
compute is needed, or when speed matters more than the exact distance. For the true
Damerau-Levenshtein distance, use [`damerauLevenshtein`](#damerauLevenshtein).

### Details

The result is the smallest number of edits that turn `left` into `right`, when no substring is
edited more than once. An edit inserts, deletes, or replaces one scalar value, or swaps two
neighbouring scalar values. Because no substring is edited twice, `"ca"` to `"abc"` is 3. The
result is never less than [`damerauLevenshtein`](#damerauLevenshtein)'s. The shorter text is processed 64 scalar
values at a time with bit operations, so the time is proportional to the longer length times
the shorter length divided by 64.

### Errors

- `OutOfMemoryError` if the `Allocator` cannot supply the scratch rows. ASCII inputs of at
  most 64 bytes each, after the shared start and end, do not allocate.

### Gotchas

The distance does not obey the triangle inequality: `"ca"` to `"ac"` is 1 and `"ac"` to
`"abc"` is 1, but `"ca"` to `"abc"` is 3.

### Examples

#### Compare the two variants

```silk
import silk.text.edit_distance
import silk.mem.allocator { Allocator, OutOfMemoryError }
import silk.core.effect { Effect }

effect fn check() -> i32 ! OutOfMemoryError ? &mut Allocator {
  let aligned = run edit_distance.optimalStringAlignment("ca", "abc")
  let exact = run edit_distance.damerauLevenshtein("ca", "abc")
  let swapped = run edit_distance.optimalStringAlignment("naïve", "nalve")
  if aligned != 3 || exact != 2 || swapped != 1 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}

effect fn exhausted(error: OutOfMemoryError) -> i32 {
  drop error
  return 2
}

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let mut allocator = Allocator.systemAllocatorProvider()
  return run Effect.catchAll(check(), exhausted) |> Effect.provideMut<Allocator>(&mut allocator)
}
```
